newsitem.title: UK: Dollar cools off in Europe as bulls take a break.
newsitem.headline: Dollar cools off in Europe as bulls take a break.

text.p: The dollar calmed down by Europe's midsession after shooting to a fresh 56-month high against the yen overnight, with traders saying bullishness was still intact but operators had judged it was time to ease off.
Some Japanese officials' comments sounding a warning on "excessive moves" in the currency market dampened the dollar slightly, but the impact of this was fleeting, traders said.

The market was focusing more on U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers' testimony before a Senate subcommittee later today in the hope that he would make some reference to the dollar's recent rally.

"This morning's been about buying on dips where you can. There are a few technicals suggesting the dollar is a bit overbought, so people are a bit nervous about driving it much higher now," said one trader at a British bank.
The dollar was at 126.34/44 yen at 1035 GMT, edging down from 126.92 hit earlier which was its highest level since August 1992. It was still above Tuesday's late European level of 126.00/05.
Against the mark it was at 1.7152/57 after being rejected just short of the 1.7200 level overnight, and compared with 1.7112/18 in Tuesday's late Europe.

The question of when and whether authorities would intervene to stem the dollar's rise was on operators' minds, but many believed that for now officials would stick to dollar-dampening comments, such as those made today.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said earlier that Japan would deal appropriately with excessive moves in the currency market.
Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Finance Ministry's international finance bureau, said intervention by Japanese authorities was possible if rates deviate greatly from economic fundamentals.
Analysts said there was not much sting in such comments as the dollar's moves were indeed in line with the economic fundamentals of the U.S., Japan and Germany.

"The trends we've seen all year are still in place... What we've seen this week in the way of (German) unemployment numbers was disappointing, and the (Bank of Japan's) Tankan survey was quite disappointing as well," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Investment Bank here.
"After three-percent growth in Japan last year it looks like this year it'll struggle to be half that, so it's very difficult to see an early change in monetary policy," Marshall said.

Such a super-easy credit policy in Japan, where interest rates are among the lowest in the world, and low rates in Germany as well were adding to the dollar's charm by making yields in U.S. markets look all the more attractive.

"Since Japan has ruled out an early discount rate hike there's just nothing there that's going to be supportive for the yen in the next few months," said Sonja Gibbs, market strategist at Nomura International here.
"If you think about the capital outflow in Japan's new fiscal year (started April 1), it's all dollar-supportive."

Meanwhile, the U.S. seems reluctant to push the dollar lower, with Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin saying after his trip to Asia this week that he had accomplished what he wanted in Japan. While in Tokyo, Rubin had said currencies should not be used as instruments of trade policy.

"The U.S. doesn't want Japan to export its way out of recession, but there aren't a lot of options available. Japan's committed to fiscal tightening and monetary policy has played out, so that really only leaves the currency," Chase's Marshall said.
